title: RAG architecture: chunking, embedding, retrieval, reranking, grounding
story:
A model knows what was in its training data. It cannot tell you where an answer came from, and it cannot be corrected without retraining. Lewis and colleagues framed the problem precisely in 2020: large pre-trained models store factual knowledge in their parameters, but their ability to access and precisely manipulate knowledge is limited, so on knowledge-intensive tasks they lag behind task-specific architectures — and providing provenance for decisions and updating world knowledge remain open problems.

Their construction splits knowledge in two. A parametric memory, which is the pre-trained sequence-to-sequence model, holds language ability. A non-parametric memory, a dense vector index accessed with a pre-trained neural retriever, holds facts. The two are combined in a probabilistic model trained end to end: for a query, a maximum inner product search finds the top documents, which are treated as a latent variable and marginalised over.

Two of their results decide how you should think about the architecture. On language generation the models produce more specific, diverse and factual language than a parametric-only baseline. And world knowledge can be updated by simply replacing the non-parametric memory — which addresses the staleness that produces outdated-fact errors, and is the property that makes this an engineering approach rather than a research one. You can fix a wrong fact by editing an index instead of retraining.

The pipeline everyone builds from this has more stages than the paper, and each is a place to lose. Chunking splits documents into retrievable units, and the size is a genuine trade: too small and a chunk lacks the context to be understood, too large and the embedding averages several topics into a vector that is near nothing in particular. Embedding maps chunks into the space where similarity is measured, which is the dot-product lesson applied — and the space is only as meaningful as the model that built it. Retrieval finds candidates. Reranking reorders them with a more expensive model that sees the query and document together, which catches what a single vector comparison cannot. Grounding assembles the retrieved text into the prompt and asks for an answer with citations.

Where it fails is the thing to carry, because it is not where people look. The generator is usually fine. Retrieval fails silently — it always returns its top results, and a top result is returned whether or not anything relevant exists. So the characteristic failure is a fluent, confident, well-cited answer built on passages that were merely the nearest available. Nothing in the chain reports that the nearest was not near.

problem.name: Retrieval-augmented generation
problem.shape: A model must answer from a body of knowledge it was not trained on, with provenance, and be correctable without retraining.
tell: the underlying facts change more often than a model can be retrained
the corpus is private or post-dates training
answers are confident and cite passages that do not support them
problem.move: Split language ability from facts: keep the model for the first and an index for the second. Then treat retrieval as the failure-prone stage — measure it separately from generation, rerank candidates with a model that sees query and document together, and require the answer to be supported by the retrieved text rather than merely accompanied by it.
problem.invariant: The system can only ground an answer in what retrieval returned, so the ceiling on answer quality is retrieval quality, and world knowledge is updated by replacing the index rather than the parameters.
problem.breaks: Retrieval returns its nearest candidates whether or not any are relevant, so absence of relevant material is indistinguishable from presence of it in the output. The failure is silent, well-formed and cited, which makes it harder to detect than a model simply being wrong.

cost.time: a search and usually a rerank before generation begins, adding latency to every answer
cost.space: the index, plus the embeddings, plus the original documents you must keep to show the citation
cost.beats: retraining, which is slow, expensive and cannot provide provenance, and a longer prompt, which is bounded and cannot search

worked.problem: Where does a retrieval-augmented system actually fail?
worked.reasoning:
At retrieval, almost always — and the reason it is hard to catch is that failure there produces a well-formed answer rather than an obvious error.

Take the structure first. The model supplies language ability, the index supplies facts, and generation is conditioned on whatever retrieval returned. So the ceiling on answer quality is retrieval quality: the generator cannot use a document it was not given, and it will do something with whatever it was given.

The specific failure mode is that retrieval always returns results. Ask for the top few passages and you receive the top few, ranked by similarity, whether or not anything in the corpus is actually relevant. There is no natural signal distinguishing the nearest passage in a corpus that contains the answer from the nearest passage in a corpus that does not. The generator then writes a fluent, confident, cited answer on top of passages that were merely closest.

That is worse than a model hallucinating unaided, because the citations make it checkable-looking. A reader sees sources attached and extends trust that the presence of sources has not earned — the passages are real, they just do not support the claim.

The upstream causes are worth separating, because they have different fixes. Chunking sets what can be retrieved at all: chunks too small lack the context to be understood on their own, and chunks too large average several topics into one vector that sits near nothing in particular. Embedding determines what similar means, and that space is only as good as the model that built it — similarity is a dot product in a space somebody else chose, which is the point the similarity lesson makes. And a single vector comparison cannot see the query and the document together, which is why reranking with a more expensive model that does see both catches cases the first pass cannot.

So what I would actually do. Measure retrieval separately from generation, because a single end-to-end score conflates two systems and attributes the failure to the wrong one — build a set of questions with known-relevant passages and score whether those passages were retrieved at all. Rerank. And require the answer to be supported by the retrieved text rather than merely accompanied by it, which means checking whether the claim appears in the cited passage and not just that a passage was cited.

The property worth remembering on the other side is the one that makes this an engineering approach: world knowledge can be updated by replacing the non-parametric memory. A wrong fact is fixed by editing an index rather than retraining, which is the whole reason this architecture is worth its complexity.

problem.practice: Take twenty real questions and record, for each, whether the passage that actually answers it was retrieved. That number is your ceiling. Then ask your system a question your corpus definitely cannot answer, and read what it does — that behaviour is what a user gets whenever retrieval misses.

beats.broke: A model knows what was in its training data, cannot tell you where an answer came from, and cannot be corrected without retraining.
beats.fix: Split knowledge in two — leave language ability in the parameters and put facts in an external index searched at question time — so answers are grounded in retrieved text that can be cited.
beats.cost: The answer is only as good as what retrieval returned, so every failure of the retriever becomes a failure of the system, and the retriever fails silently by returning plausible but irrelevant passages.
